s0101.literal: The Way and Buddhism were appended separately, nine sections in all.
s0101.idiomatic: Daoism and Buddhism were listed in appendices, nine sections in all.

s0102.literal: Yet he still did not set forth the authors' intentions; he only established a biography beneath each book title, and also composed nine articles of regulations, compiled in the first scroll.
s0102.idiomatic: Yet he still did not explain the authors' intentions; he only added a biographical note under each title, and also wrote nine articles of regulations placed in the first scroll.

s0103.literal: The literary meaning was shallow and recent, and did not serve as a standard.
s0103.idiomatic: The prose was shallow and recent, and did not serve as a proper standard.

s0104.literal: In the Yongming era of Qi, Secretariat Assistant Wang Liang and Superintendent Xie Tiao also compiled the Four-Section Book List; in all, eighteen thousand ten scrolls.
s0104.idiomatic: During the Yongming era of Qi, Secretariat Assistant Wang Liang and Superintendent Xie Tiao also compiled the Four-Section Book List, totaling eighteen thousand ten scrolls.

s0105.literal: At the end of Qi, war and fire spread to the secret pavilion, and the classics and records were lost and scattered.
s0105.idiomatic: At the end of Qi, war and fire spread to the secret pavilion, and the classics and records were lost and scattered.

s0106.literal: At the beginning of Liang, Superintendent Ren Fang personally undertook the classification, and also arranged the collected books within the Hall of Cultured Virtue; in the Hua Lin Garden he gathered Buddhist scriptures together—in all, twenty-three thousand one hundred sixty scrolls, not counting Buddhist texts.
s0106.idiomatic: At the beginning of Liang, Superintendent Ren Fang personally undertook the classification and arranged the collected books in the Hall of Cultured Virtue. In the Hua Lin Garden he gathered Buddhist scriptures together—twenty-three thousand one hundred sixty scrolls in all, not counting Buddhist texts.

s0107.literal: Liang had the Four-Section Catalog by Superintendents Ren Fang and Yin Jun, and also the Hall of Cultured Virtue Catalog.
s0107.idiomatic: The Liang dynasty produced the Four-Section Catalog by Superintendents Ren Fang and Yin Jun, and also the Hall of Cultured Virtue Catalog.

s0108.literal: Books on numerology were made into a separate section, with Attendant-in-Ordinary Zu Geng assigned to compile its titles.
s0108.idiomatic: Books on numerology were placed in a separate section, with Attendant-in-Ordinary Zu Geng assigned to compile its titles.

s0109.literal: Thus Liang had the Five-Section Catalog.
s0109.idiomatic: Thus the Liang dynasty had the Five-Section Catalog.

s0110.literal: In the Putong era there was the recluse Ruan Xiaoxu, quiet and free of desire, who deeply loved ancient texts and history, broadly gathered book records from the houses of kings and nobles since Song and Qi, cross-checked them against official registers, and further compiled the Seven Records: first, the Record of Classics, recording the Six Arts;
s0110.idiomatic: In the Putong era there was the recluse Ruan Xiaoxu, quiet and free of desire, who deeply loved ancient texts and history. He broadly gathered book records from noble households since Song and Qi, cross-checked them against official registers, and compiled the Seven Records: first, the Record of Classics, recording the Six Arts;

s0111.literal: second, the Record of Annals and Biographies, recording histories and biographies;
s0111.idiomatic: second, the Record of Annals and Biographies, recording histories and biographies;

s0112.literal: third, the Record of Masters and Military Books, recording masters' texts and military books;
s0112.idiomatic: third, the Record of Masters and Military Books, recording philosophical texts and military books;

s0113.literal: fourth, the Record of Literary Collections, recording odes and rhapsodies;
s0113.idiomatic: fourth, the Record of Literary Collections, recording odes and rhapsodies;

s0114.literal: fifth, the Record of Technical Arts, recording numerology;
s0114.idiomatic: fifth, the Record of Technical Arts, recording numerology;

s0117.literal: Its division of sections and titles had a certain order, but its analysis of meaning was shallow and unsound.
s0117.idiomatic: Its division of sections and titles had a certain order, but its analysis of meaning was shallow and unsound.

s0118.literal: Emperor Wu of Liang deeply delighted in the Odes and Documents and transformed those below through his example above; within the four borders, every household had literary and historical books.
s0118.idiomatic: Emperor Wu of Liang deeply delighted in the Odes and Documents and set an example from above; within the four borders, every household had literary and historical books.

s0119.literal: When Emperor Yuan defeated Hou Jing, he collected the books of the Hall of Cultured Virtue and public and private classics and records, bringing them back to Jiangling—in all, more than seventy thousand scrolls.
s0119.idiomatic: When Emperor Yuan defeated Hou Jing, he collected the books of the Hall of Cultured Virtue along with public and private classics and records, bringing them back to Jiangling—more than seventy thousand scrolls in all.

s0120.literal: When the Zhou army entered Ying, they were all burned.
s0120.idiomatic: When the Zhou army entered Ying, they were all burned.

s0121.literal: In the Tianchen era of Chen, they again gathered and reassembled books, but examining the titles, many were still missing.
s0121.idiomatic: In the Tianchen era of Chen, they again gathered and reassembled books, but examining the titles, many were still missing.

s0122.literal: Among them, in the Central Plains war followed war and arms were the chief concern; only under Former Qin and Later Qin did literary culture flourish.
s0122.idiomatic: In the Central Plains, war followed war and arms were the chief concern; only under Former Qin and Later Qin did literary culture flourish.

s0123.literal: When Emperor Wu of Song entered the passes, he collected their charts and records; what the treasury held amounted to only four thousand scrolls.
s0123.idiomatic: When Emperor Wu of Song entered the passes, he collected their charts and records; the treasury held only four thousand scrolls.

s0124.literal: Red axles and blue paper; the writing was ancient and crude.
s0124.idiomatic: They had red axles and blue paper, and the writing was ancient and crude.

s0125.literal: Later Wei first established its capital at Yan and Dai, pushed south into the Central Plains, and roughly collected classics and histories, but could not fully assemble them.
s0125.idiomatic: Later Wei first established its capital at Yan and Dai, pushed south into the Central Plains, and roughly collected classics and histories, but could not fully assemble them.

s0126.literal: When Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital to Luoyang, he borrowed books from Qi, and the secret repository gradually became fuller.
s0126.idiomatic: When Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital to Luoyang, he borrowed books from Qi, and the secret repository gradually became fuller.

s0127.literal: By the time of the Erzhu turmoil, they were scattered among the people.
s0127.idiomatic: By the time of the Erzhu turmoil, they were scattered among the people.

s0128.literal: Later, when Northern Qi moved to Ye, they searched and gathered further; down to the Tiantong and Wuping eras, collation and copying never ceased.
s0128.idiomatic: Later, when Northern Qi moved to Ye, they searched and gathered further; down to the Tiantong and Wuping eras, collation and copying never ceased.

s0129.literal: Later Zhou first established its base in the Guanzhong region, pressed from without by powerful neighbors, with war-horses in the suburbs and no leisure even for a day's work.
s0129.idiomatic: Later Zhou first established its base in the Guanzhong region, pressed from without by powerful neighbors, with war-horses in the suburbs and no leisure even for a day's work.

s0130.literal: At the beginning of the Baoding era, books numbered only eight thousand; afterward they were gradually increased until they barely reached ten thousand scrolls.
s0130.idiomatic: At the beginning of the Baoding era, books numbered only eight thousand; afterward they were gradually increased until they barely reached ten thousand scrolls.

s0131.literal: When Emperor Wu of Zhou conquered Northern Qi, he first sealed the book repository; the old texts added amounted to only five thousand.
s0131.idiomatic: When Emperor Wu of Zhou conquered Northern Qi, he first sealed the book repository; the old texts added amounted to only five thousand.

s0132.literal: In Sui, Superintendent of the Secretariat Niu Hong submitted a memorial requesting that emissaries be dispatched separately to search for variant copies.
s0132.idiomatic: In Sui, Superintendent of the Secretariat Niu Hong submitted a memorial requesting that emissaries be dispatched separately to search for variant copies.

s0133.literal: For each scroll of a book, one bolt of silk was given as reward; once collation and copying were finished, the original was returned to its owner.
s0133.idiomatic: For each scroll of a book, one bolt of silk was given as reward; once collation and copying were finished, the original was returned to its owner.

s0134.literal: Thereupon variant books among the people often appeared from time to time.
s0134.idiomatic: Thereupon variant books among the people often appeared from time to time.

s0135.literal: After Chen was pacified, the classics and records gradually became complete.
s0135.idiomatic: After Chen was pacified, the classics and records gradually became complete.

s0136.literal: Examining what was obtained, most were books from the Taijian era; the paper and ink were poor, and the writing was also crude and bad.
s0136.idiomatic: Examining what was obtained, most were books from the Taijian era; the paper and ink were poor, and the writing was also crude and bad.

s0137.literal: Thereupon they were gathered together, arranged in order, and preserved as old texts.
s0137.idiomatic: Thereupon they were gathered together, arranged in order, and preserved as old texts.

s0138.literal: They summoned masters of calligraphy from throughout the realm—Wei Pei of Jingzhao, Du Yun of Nanyang, and others—and within the Secretariat supplemented and restored what was missing, making principal and duplicate copies stored in the palace; the rest filled the inner and outer pavilions of the Secretariat—in all, more than thirty thousand scrolls.
s0138.idiomatic: They summoned masters of calligraphy from throughout the realm—Wei Pei of Jingzhao, Du Yun of Nanyang, and others—and within the Secretariat supplemented and restored what was missing, making principal and duplicate copies stored in the palace. The rest filled the inner and outer pavilions of the Secretariat—more than thirty thousand scrolls in all.

s0139.literal: When Emperor Yang ascended the throne, books in the secret pavilion were limited to fifty copied sets, divided into three grades: top grade with red glass axles, middle grade with dark blue glass axles, and lower grade with lacquer axles.
s0139.idiomatic: When Emperor Yang ascended the throne, books in the secret pavilion were limited to fifty copied sets, divided into three grades: top grade with red glass axles, middle grade with dark blue glass axles, and lower grade with lacquer axles.

s0140.literal: At the Eastern Capital's Hall for Viewing Literature, buildings were constructed in the east and west wings to store them: the east wing stored sections A and B, the west wing stored sections C and D.
s0140.idiomatic: At the Eastern Capital's Hall for Viewing Literature, buildings were constructed in the east and west wings to store them: the east wing stored sections A and B, the west wing stored sections C and D.

s0141.literal: They also gathered ancient traces and famous paintings since Wei, and behind the hall erected two platforms: the east was called the Platform of Exquisite Models, storing ancient traces;
s0141.idiomatic: They also gathered ancient traces and famous paintings since Wei, and behind the hall erected two platforms: the east was called the Platform of Exquisite Models, storing ancient traces;

s0142.literal: the west was called the Platform of Precious Traces, storing ancient paintings.
s0142.idiomatic: the west was called the Platform of Precious Traces, storing ancient paintings.

s0143.literal: They also gathered Daoist and Buddhist scriptures at the Inner Way Place and separately compiled a catalog.
s0143.idiomatic: They also gathered Daoist and Buddhist scriptures at the Inner Way Place and separately compiled a catalog.

s0144.literal: When the Great Tang conquered the false Zheng regime, it fully collected their charts, books, and ancient traces.
s0144.idiomatic: When the Great Tang conquered the false Zheng regime, it fully collected their charts, books, and ancient traces.

s0145.literal: He ordered Vice Director of the Directorate of Agriculture Song Zungui to load them onto boats and send them up the Yellow River westward, intending to bring them to the capital.
s0145.idiomatic: He ordered Vice Director of the Directorate of Agriculture Song Zungui to load them onto boats and send them up the Yellow River westward, intending to bring them to the capital.

s0146.literal: Passing Di Gorge, many were washed away and sunk; of what survived, not one in ten remained.
s0146.idiomatic: Passing Di Gorge, many were washed away and sunk; of what survived, not one in ten remained.

s0147.literal: The Catalog was also gradually soaked by the water, and at times had gaps and omissions.
s0147.idiomatic: The Catalog was also gradually soaked by the water, and at times had gaps and omissions.

s0148.literal: Now examining what survives, they are divided into four sections, combined into fourteen thousand four hundred sixty-six titles, with eighty-nine thousand six hundred sixty-six scrolls.
s0148.idiomatic: Now examining what survives, they are divided into four sections, combined into fourteen thousand four hundred sixty-six titles, with eighty-nine thousand six hundred sixty-six scrolls.

s0149.literal: What the old register took in but whose meaning was shallow and vulgar and of no benefit to teaching and principle—all were deleted.
s0149.idiomatic: Entries from the old register whose meaning was shallow and vulgar and of no benefit to teaching and principle were all deleted.

s0150.literal: What the old register omitted but whose meaning was worth adopting and could broaden and benefit—all were appended.
s0150.idiomatic: Entries the old register omitted but whose meaning was worth adopting and could broaden and benefit were all appended.

s0151.literal: Looking far at the histories of Sima and Ban, and near at the records and catalogs of Wang and Ruan, drawing on their style and structure, cutting away the frivolous, vulgar, and coarse, separating what was remote, joining what was close and dense, condensing the text and clarifying the meaning—in all fifty-five sections, each listed under its own entry, to complete the Bibliographic Treatise.
s0151.idiomatic: Looking far at the histories of Sima Qian and Ban Gu, and near at the records and catalogs of Wang and Ruan, I drew on their style and structure, cut away the frivolous, vulgar, and coarse, separated what was remote, joined what was close and dense, and condensed the text and clarified the meaning—in all fifty-five sections, each listed under its own entry, to complete the Bibliographic Treatise.

s0152.literal: Although I have not been able to probe the subtle and explore the hidden, reaching the utmost depths, I hope that in spreading the Way and establishing teaching nothing may be left out.
s0152.idiomatic: Although I have not been able to probe the subtle and explore the hidden, reaching the utmost depths, I hope that in spreading the Way and establishing teaching nothing may be left out.

s0153.literal: Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom are what govern the state; technical arts and numerology are what govern the body;
s0153.idiomatic: Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom are what govern the state; technical arts and numerology are what govern the body;

s0154.literal: The various masters are the heralds of the classics and records, and literary writings are the adornments of government and transformation—all are instruments of governance.
s0154.idiomatic: The various masters are the heralds of the classics and records, and literary writings are the adornments of government and transformation—all are instruments of governance.

s0155.literal: Therefore they are listed in this treatise.
s0155.idiomatic: Therefore they are listed in this treatise.

s0156.literal: Classic: Changes—The Hidden Storehouse, thirteen scrolls, annotated by Xue Zhen, Grand Commandant's Aide of Jin.
s0156.idiomatic: Classic: Changes—The Hidden Storehouse, thirteen scrolls, annotated by Xue Zhen, Grand Commandant's Aide of Jin.

s0157.literal: The Book of Changes, two scrolls, transmitted by Bu Zixia, teacher of Marquis Wen of Wei, incomplete.
s0157.idiomatic: The Book of Changes, two scrolls, transmitted by Bu Zixia, teacher of Marquis Wen of Wei, incomplete.

s0158.literal: The Liang catalog had six scrolls.
s0158.idiomatic: The Liang catalog listed six scrolls.

s0159.literal: The Book of Changes, ten scrolls, with commentarial glosses by Jing Fang, Administrator of Wei Commandery in Han.
s0159.idiomatic: The Book of Changes, ten scrolls, with commentarial glosses by Jing Fang, Administrator of Wei Commandery in Han.

s0160.literal: The Book of Changes, eight scrolls, with commentarial glosses by Meng Xi, Director of the Qu Terrace in Han, incomplete.
s0160.idiomatic: The Book of Changes, eight scrolls, with commentarial glosses by Meng Xi, Director of the Qu Terrace in Han, incomplete.

s0161.literal: The Liang catalog had ten scrolls.
s0161.idiomatic: The Liang catalog listed ten scrolls.

s0162.literal: There was also Fei Zhi's commentary on the Book of Changes in four scrolls, by the Chief of Shanfu in Han, lost.
s0162.idiomatic: There was also Fei Zhi's commentary on the Book of Changes in four scrolls, by the Chief of Shanfu in Han, lost.

s0163.literal: The Book of Changes, nine scrolls, annotated by Zheng Xuan, Grand Minister of Agriculture of Later Han.
s0163.idiomatic: The Book of Changes, nine scrolls, annotated by Zheng Xuan, Grand Minister of Agriculture of Later Han.

s0164.literal: The Liang catalog also had Ma Rong's commentary on the Book of Changes in one scroll, by the Administrator of Nan Commandery in Han, lost.
s0164.idiomatic: The Liang catalog also listed Ma Rong's commentary on the Book of Changes in one scroll, by the Administrator of Nan Commandery in Han, lost.

s0165.literal: The Book of Changes, five scrolls, with commentarial glosses by Liu Biao, Governor of Jing Province in Han.
s0165.idiomatic: The Book of Changes, five scrolls, with commentarial glosses by Liu Biao, Governor of Jing Province in Han.

s0166.literal: The Liang catalog had Song Zhong's commentary on the Book of Changes in ten scrolls, by an Attendant in the Five Professions of Jing Province in Han, lost.
s0166.idiomatic: The Liang catalog listed Song Zhong's commentary on the Book of Changes in ten scrolls, by an Attendant in the Five Professions of Jing Province in Han, lost.

s0167.literal: The Book of Changes, eleven scrolls, annotated by Xun Shuang, Minister of Works in Han.
s0167.idiomatic: The Book of Changes, eleven scrolls, annotated by Xun Shuang, Minister of Works in Han.

s0168.literal: The Book of Changes, ten scrolls, annotated by Wang Su, General of the Guard in Wei.
s0168.idiomatic: The Book of Changes, ten scrolls, annotated by Wang Su, General of the Guard in Wei.

s0169.literal: The Book of Changes, ten scrolls: Wang Bi of Wei, Gentleman of the Masters of Writing, annotated the Sixty-Four Hexagrams in six scrolls; Han Kangbo annotated the Appended Statements and below in three scrolls; Wang Bi also composed An Outline of the Changes in one scroll. The Liang catalog had Dong Yu's commentary on the Book of Changes in ten scrolls, by the Grand Minister of Agriculture of Wei, and Xun Hui's commentary on the Book of Changes in ten scrolls, by the Regular Attendant of the Palace in Wei, lost.
s0169.idiomatic: The Book of Changes, ten scrolls: Wang Bi of Wei, Gentleman of the Masters of Writing, annotated the Sixty-Four Hexagrams in six scrolls; Han Kangbo annotated the Appended Statements and below in three scrolls; Wang Bi also composed An Outline of the Changes in one scroll. s0170.idiomatic: The Book of Changes, ten scrolls, annotated by Yao Xin, Grand Minister of Ceremonies of Wu.
